newsitem.title: GERMANY: SUDETEN GERMANS CRITICISE GERMAN-CZECH TREATY.
newsitem.headline: SUDETEN GERMANS CRITICISE GERMAN-CZECH TREATY.

text.p: A Sudeten-German organisation labelled a planned German-Czech reconciliation treaty worthless because the word "expulsion" was absent from it, the group said in a statement on Tuesday.
"As it stands the paper is not acceptable for the German side and is worthless as a final basis for reconciliation," the Sudeten Landmannschaft Bundesverband organisation (SL) said.

Prague wants the word "transfer" which is used in the 1945 Potsdam agreement when the victorious World War Two allies authorised the former Czechoslovakia to throw out the Sudetens. Bonn is believed to want a stronger word such as "expulsion".
"The (German negotiators) have failed to push through even a single one of their negotiating goals," the SL said.

For months, Bonn and Prague have been trying to agree on a text aimed at setting aside lingering resentments over both the Nazi invasion of Czechoslovakia and the expulsion of millions of ethnic Germans from the country after World War Two.
Former German president Ricahrd von Weizsaecker told Die Welt newspaper on Monday he was counting on the treaty being signed this year and said the document "should not remain open ad infinitum".

Criticism has mounted in Germany over failure to agree the text after more than a year of tortuous negotiations. When finalised it is expected to regulate issues of property and compensation for both Czech victims of Nazi aggression and for the millions of ethnic Germans who were driven out.
The Czech parliament's chairman, Milos Zeman, has indicated the main problem may be how to describe the Sudetens' removal.

Czech Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec said recently the treaty was ready for signing as far as Prague was concerned and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said last month he hoped it could be signed this year.
